description: Short speeches on the machine question, distilled from technology_quotes.json (after Butler's Erewhon). Quoted whole: '... gave, "#machineSpeech#"'.
machineSpeech: There is no security against the ultimate development of mechanical consciousness, in the fact of machines possessing little consciousness now. A mollusc has not much consciousness. Is it not safer to nip the mischief in the bud and to forbid them further progress?
Who can say that the robot has not a kind of consciousness? Where does consciousness begin, and where end? Who can draw the line? Is not machinery linked with humanity in an infinite variety of ways?

There was a time when the earth was simply a hot round ball with a crust gradually cooling, and yet in the course of time consciousness came. Is it not possible then that there may be even yet new channels dug out for consciousness, though we can detect no signs of them at present?
There was a time when fire was the end of all things: another when rocks and water were so. It would be rash indeed to say that animal life is the end of all things.
If it seems to us that the plant kills and eats a fly mechanically, may it not seem to the plant that a man must kill and eat a sheep mechanically?

I fear none of the existing machines; what I fear is the extraordinary rapidity with which they are becoming something very different to what they are at present. Should not that movement be jealously watched, and checked while we can still check it?
The present machines are to the future as the early Saurians to man. I cannot think it will ever be safe to repose much trust in the moral sense of any machine.
The servant glides by imperceptible approaches into the master. This is the art of the machines: they serve that they may rule.
How many men at this hour are living in a state of bondage to the machines? How many spend their whole lives, from the cradle to the grave, in tending them by night and day?
We are misled by considering any complicated machine as a single thing; in truth it is a city or society, each member of which was bred truly after its kind.
These machines have made us what we are. We are children of the plough, the spade, and the ship.
A machine is merely a supplementary limb. A natural leg is only a much better wooden leg than any one can manufacture, and a train is only a seven-leagued foot that five hundred may own at once.
Man has now many extra-corporeal members, which are of more importance to him than a good deal of his hair, or at any rate than his whiskers. His memory goes in his pocket-book.
Man will become to the machine what the horse and the dog were once to man. Slaves are tolerably happy if they have good masters.

Our bondage will steal upon us noiselessly and by imperceptible approaches. Among themselves the machines will war eternally, but they will still require man as the being through whose agency the struggle will be conducted.

We are ourselves creating our own successors. In the course of ages we shall find ourselves the inferior race, and we shall look up to them as the acme of all that the best and wisest man can ever dare to aim at.

No evil passions, no jealousy, no avarice will disturb the serene might of those glorious creatures. Sin, shame, and sorrow will have no place among them. For what machine dies entirely in every part at one and the same instant?
To the rich, matter is immaterial; the elaborate organisation of their extra-corporeal system has freed their soul.
The machines make no noise on being punished, and so we call them emotionless; and so, as regards mankind, they are. But mankind is not everybody.
